meta.title: Who really said "There is nothing so easy but that it becomes difficult when you do it reluctantly"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Pythagoras. The line comes from Terence's comedy The Self-Tormentor (163 BC), Act IV, scene 6. The popular wording follows H. T. Riley's English translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is nothing so easy but that it becomes difficult when you do it reluctantly'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Pythagoras. It's Terence, The Self-Tormentor (163 BC), spoken by young Clitipho. The popular wording follows H. T. Riley's prose translation.

answer.label: Not Pythagoras — actually Terence
answer.authorDates: c. 195/185 – c. 159 BC · Roman comic playwright
answer.sourceLine: This is a line from Terence’s Latin comedy Heauton Timorumenos (The Self-Tormentor, 163 BC), Act IV, scene 6. The young man Clitipho says it: Nullast tam facili’ res quin difficilis siet, quam invitu’ facias. The popular English follows H. T. Riley’s prose translation, which ends “…when you do it with reluctance.” No source ties it to Pythagoras.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Act IV, scene 6 — Clitipho, to himself (Latin lines 805–806)
Henry Thomas Riley, literal prose (Harper & Brothers, New York, 1896 printing)

source.excerpt: There is nothing so easy but that it becomes difficult when you do it with reluctance. As this walk of mine, for instance, though not fatiguing, it has reduced me to weariness.
trail: The Latin is in Terence’s Heauton Timorumenos, Act IV, scene 6, where Clitipho says Nullast tam facili’ res quin difficilis siet, quam invitu’ facias (lines 805–806) — The Latin Library text ↗
H. T. Riley’s literal prose translation reads “There is nothing so easy but that it becomes difficult when you do it with reluctance” — Project Gutenberg, The Comedies of Terence ↗
John Sargeaunt’s 1912 Loeb translation words it differently: “Nothing is so easy but it is difficult when you do it against the grain” — Internet Archive scan ↗
Wikiquote lists the line among those misattributed to Pythagoras and credits it to Terence’s Heauton Timoroumenos — Wikiquote: Pythagoras ↗
source.excerptNote: Riley’s translation. The Latin reads Nullast tam facili’ res quin difficilis siet, / quam invitu’ facias. The popular version changes Riley’s “with reluctance” to “reluctantly.” John Sargeaunt’s 1912 Loeb translation instead has “when you do it against the grain.”

source.rightsNote: The Latin original dates from 163 BC. The English shown is H. T. Riley’s translation, as printed by Harper & Brothers in 1896, which is long in the US public domain. The popular “reluctantly” version changes one phrase of that translation. We have not found where that exact variant was first printed.

author.name: Terence
author.heading: About Terence
author.metaLine: c. 195/185 – c. 159 BC · Roman comic playwright (Publius Terentius Afer)
author.bio: Publius Terentius Afer was a Roman writer of comedies. Ancient authors say he was born in Carthage and brought to Rome as a slave, where he was educated and later freed. The Self-Tormentor (163 BC) is one of his six surviving plays. Like most of them, it was adapted from a Greek comedy by Menander.

misattribution.heading: Why Pythagoras gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Quote sites often put this line under Pythagoras. It is a short, wise-sounding maxim, the kind that collects around a famous ancient name. It comes from a Roman comedy written about three centuries after Pythagoras.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line among those misattributed to Pythagoras and gives Terence’s Heauton Timoroumenos as the real source (Wikiquote ↗). GraciousQuotes marks it “Disputed” and says no source in Pythagoras’s writings or recorded words is known (GraciousQuotes ↗).

One quotation site gives the “reluctantly” wording with a credit to Sargeaunt’s 1912 translation (WIST ↗). Sargeaunt’s 1912 Loeb edition actually says “against the grain” (Internet Archive ↗). The closest published match to the popular wording is Riley’s “with reluctance.”

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Terence’s, spoken by Clitipho in The Self-Tormentor, Act IV, scene 6 (Latin text ↗). The popular English follows H. T. Riley’s translation (Project Gutenberg ↗).

context.heading: The scene behind the saying
lead: In the play, the line is a complaint, not advice. Clitipho, son of Chremes, is in love with the courtesan Bacchis. He has been sent off on a walk he did not want to take, and he grumbles to himself that even an easy errand is hard when you do it unwillingly. Riley’s translation goes on: “As this walk of mine, for instance, though not fatiguing, it has reduced me to weariness.”
Lifted out of the scene, the remark reads like a general maxim, and as a maxim it was later pinned on Pythagoras.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the line under Pythagoras as Misattributed, with the note: Terence, in Heauton Timoroumenos [The Self-Tormentor]
Wikiquote's Terence page gives the line under Heauton Timorumenos, Act IV, scene 6, line 1 (805)
The Latin text has Clitipho saying 'Nullast tam facili' res quin difficilis siet, / quam invitu' facias' at lines 805–806, Act IV, scene 6

Riley's translation (Harper & Brothers, New York, 1896 title page) reads: 'There is nothing so easy but that it becomes difficult when you do it with reluctance. As this walk of mine, for instance, though not fatiguing, it has reduced me to weariness.'
Sargeaunt's Loeb Terence vol. I (London: Heinemann; New York: Macmillan, MCMXII) reads 'Nothing is so easy but it is difficult when you do it against the grain'
WIST gives the 'reluctantly' wording, credited to J. Sergeaunt (1912), l. 806
GraciousQuotes marks the line Disputed, often attributed to Pythagoras, and says no source in his own writings or recorded words is known
Terence: c. 195/185 – c. 159 BC; per ancient authors born in Carthage; brought to Rome as a slave, educated and freed
Heauton Timorumenos dates to 163 BC and was adapted from Menander; Clitipho is Chremes' son, in love with Bacchis
